transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, thank you. Yeah, so... well, honestly, it took me a while to actually make this appointment because, you know, life gets so incredibly busy, especially with my job. I'm a software developer, and right now we are in the middle of this massive project rollout, which means endless, and I mean absolutely endless, meetings. But what finally pushed me to come in—what really made me think, 'okay, I need to talk to a professional about this'—is that I just keep getting up during these really important moments when I know I should just stay put. 

Like, during our sprint planning meetings, which are crucial for my team to figure out our workload for the next two weeks, I'll just stand up and walk away from my desk. Or, on a personal front, we're dealing with some real estate stuff right now, so we have these incredibly dense mortgage calls. And right in the middle of the loan officer explaining escrow or interest rates or whatever, I’ll just... get up. I'll suddenly feel this intense, undeniable need to go get a glass of water, or I'll suddenly decide that I urgently need to check something in the other room, like if I left a specific pen on the kitchen counter. 

And I know I should just sit there and listen, I really do, but it's like my body just decides to move before my brain can stop it. I'll just wander off into the hallway, and then I realize I've missed half of what they were saying. It's just so frustrating because I'm 40 years old, I have a career, I should be able to sit through a professional call without wandering off, you know? It's just been happening so much lately, and it's starting to get embarrassing when I have to ask people to repeat themselves because I was in the other room looking for a notebook I didn't even need...

Right before you get up and walk away, are you feeling anxious or worried about something specific being discussed, or does it feel more like a sudden urge to move or get distracted by something else, without a particular worry attached?

Well, see, that's the thing that is so confusing about it. It’s definitely not anxiety. I mean, sure, dealing with escrow and mortgages is stressful for anyone, and sprint planning can be a massive headache when we have tight deadlines, but when I get up, it’s not because I’m panicking about the numbers or trying to escape a scary conversation. It’s... it’s hard to explain, but it's entirely physical. It’s this intense, bubbling feeling that just kind of takes over. 

Like, I’ll be sitting there, right? And maybe to my manager on the Zoom camera, or to my husband sitting right next to me at the table, I look totally fine. I look like I’m just quietly listening. But inside? Even when I’m sitting completely calmly on the outside, I feel this incredible pressure inside, like I absolutely need to move, or switch tasks, or just do something with my hands before I literally crawl out of my skin. 

It’s almost like a wind-up toy that’s been wound way too tight, and the energy just has to go somewhere immediately. So I’m not running away from a worry at all, I’m just... I just can't contain that physical urge. I try to suppress it, I really do, I'll grip the edges of my chair or press my feet into the floor, but then the pressure just builds and builds and builds until my brain just says 'go,' and suddenly I'm in the hallway. It's just this constant, exhausting hum of needing to be in motion, regardless of what we're actually talking about.
Thinking back to when you were a child in school, did you have similar trouble staying seated or a strong urge to get up and move around during class or other quiet activities?

Oh, wow, yeah... going back to when I was a kid... you know, it's funny you ask that because I was just talking to my mom about this the other day. We were going through some old boxes in her attic, looking for these vintage ornaments she wanted to pass down to me, and we actually found some of my old report cards from elementary school. And... yeah, it was all right there in black and white. 

I mean, I always knew I was a handful as a kid, but seeing it written out by my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was this very strict, older woman who always wore these brightly colored cardigans—it really brought it all back. She had actually written, in this very neat cursive, that she had to keep moving my desk. First, I was in the back, then I was in the front row right next to her desk, all because I just could not stay in my seat. I was always popping up to sharpen my pencil, or to look out the window, or to see what the kid next to me was drawing. 

And it wasn't just the staying seated part, either. The report cards were full of comments about how I would just blurt out answers. Like, I knew the material, I was actually a really smart kid, I understood the math worksheets and the reading assignments perfectly fine, but I would just rush through everything so fast. I’d finish my worksheet in five minutes, and then because I was done, I’d just start talking to whoever was near me, completely ignoring the fact that everyone else was still quietly working. Or the teacher would ask a question, and before she even finished the sentence, or before anyone else could even raise their hand, I’d just shout out the answer. 

It was like my brain was moving at a hundred miles an hour, and my mouth and my body just had to keep up with it. I remember getting in trouble so many times for talking out of turn. They’d always say, 'Raise your hand and wait to be called on,' and I would try, I really would, but the answer would just bubble up and explode out of me before I could even think about raising my hand. So, yeah, I guess this whole... this whole inability to just sit still and be quiet when I'm supposed to, it’s definitely not a new thing. It’s been happening since I was little, even when I totally understood what was going on in class. It’s just so exhausting to realize I’m still doing the exact same thing at forty that I was doing at eight, you know?

Aside from the urge to get up and move, do you often find it hard to keep your attention on tasks or conversations, like losing track of details, forgetting things, or getting easily distracted, even when you're sitting still?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. That is... honestly, that's just as much of a struggle as the physical restlessness, maybe even more so because it's invisible, you know? 

Like, I will sit down at my desk, and I will pull up a pull request from one of the junior devs on my team. And reviewing code is so important right now with this massive rollout we're doing, so I really do go into it with the absolute best intentions. I tell myself, 'Okay, I am going to sit here, I'm going to focus, and I'm going to read this and give good feedback.' Or, you know, going back to the real estate stuff, I'll sit down at the kitchen table with those huge, thick packets of mortgage documents that the lender sent over. I'm completely still, I'm looking right at the page, I'm reading the words... but then, after just a few minutes, I'll suddenly snap to and realize I'm just staring at the exact same section I was looking at five minutes ago. 

I haven't actually processed a single word because my brain has just gone off in a million different directions. I'll be sitting there staring at a block of code or a clause about property taxes, but in my head, I'm thinking about, like, five completely unrelated things all at once. I'll be wondering if I remembered to switch the laundry to the dryer before my next meeting, and then worrying about whether we need to pick up more coffee beans, and then trying to remember if I ever responded to a Slack message from my manager yesterday, and suddenly I'm debating what color we should paint the new guest bathroom. 

It's like my eyes are doing the physical work of reading, but my brain has just completely left the building. And then I have to force myself to go back to the top of the page and start the whole thing over again. Sometimes it takes me three or four tries just to get through one single page of a contract, which is ridiculous. It just makes every single task take so much longer than it should, and it's exhausting because I really am trying to pay attention, I really am, but my mind just will not stay on the track I put it on.
Have you also noticed times when, along with this restlessness, you felt unusually elated, needed much less sleep than normal, or had racing thoughts that lasted for several days in a row?

Oh, no, definitely not that. Like, unusually elated? Not at all. I mean, sure, I get happy when we finally ship a big software update at work after weeks of crunch time, or, you know, when the lender told us our escrow was fully funded. That felt great! But it’s not like this weird, out-of-nowhere euphoria, you know? It’s just normal, everyday happiness that makes sense for the situation. 

And the sleep thing... gosh, no, absolutely not. I need my sleep so much. If anything, my brain being so busy and distracted all day makes me completely, utterly exhausted by the time night rolls around. I’ll admit, sometimes it takes me a minute to actually fall asleep because my brain is still doing that thing where it bounces between the code I was writing and whether we need to buy more paper towels, but I definitely don't feel like I need less sleep. If I don't get my full seven or eight hours, I am just a total zombie the next morning. I'll be sitting in our daily stand-up meeting on Zoom, clutching my coffee mug just trying to keep my eyes open. I definitely don't have those days where I wake up after two hours feeling like I could run a marathon. 

And as for the racing thoughts lasting for several days in a row... I mean, my thoughts are always kind of bouncing around, like I said, but it’s not like a specific period that starts and stops over a few days. It’s just... every day. It's just my normal, everyday baseline. It never feels like this intense, unstoppable high where my thoughts are racing because I feel like I can conquer the world or anything like that. It’s just that annoying, constant distraction of wondering about the laundry and the Slack messages. So, yeah, I really haven't noticed anything like what you're describing. It’s just the same old everyday restlessness, not some big, dramatic shift in my mood or my sleep schedule.
